transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hey, doc. Uh, yeah, thanks. I guess I’m here because... well, lately I’ll get off a really long shift at the garage—I work on diesel engines, mostly big rigs and city buses. Man, the buses are the worst. You wouldn’t believe the grease buildup on those transit ones. We had this one come in last Tuesday, transmission was completely shot, and the smell... anyway, my boss expects me to just crank these out, right? 

So I get off work, or I finish up some certification studying I'm trying to do, and I just end up eating way, way more than I planned. Like, I’ll smash a full fast-food meal, then move on to snacks, and basically just eat whatever’s in the fridge, all in one sitting. Which reminds me, my fridge has this weird hum lately, might be the compressor going out. I should probably look at that, but I barely have the energy after wrenching all day, you know? But yeah, the eating thing is getting pretty out of hand.
Do you usually feel stressed, anxious, or upset before these episodes of eating a lot?

I don't really know if I'm stressed or upset right before, honestly. I haven't really paid much attention to my mood right at that exact minute. I mean, my brain is usually just totally fried by the time I clock out. 

Speaking of fried, the wiring harness on that transit bus I was telling you about? Completely melted. I swear the driver must have ignored the dash warnings for, like, fifty miles. You see that a lot with the city guys, they just push the rigs until they literally start smoking and they have no choice but to pull over. I spent three hours yesterday just splicing in new connections because the whole terminal block was fused together into this giant plastic lump. It's a nightmare trying to trace those schematics. 

But, uh... yeah, to answer your question, I don't really know how I'm feeling before I start eating. I just get home and it happens.
Do you feel like you can stop eating once you've started on those occasions?

No, man, not at all. Once I start on those nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food even while I’m telling myself to stop. And I'll be sitting there, already feeling sick to my stomach, but I just keep going. It's like I'm on autopilot or something. 

Kind of like this one guy at the shop, Dave. Dave’s been there for like twenty years, right? The guy is practically a machine himself. He can tear down an Allison transmission blindfolded, I swear. But the other day, he was pulling a heavy-duty axle out of a Peterbilt, and he didn't secure the jack right. The whole thing slipped. Bam. Pinched his hand right between the axle and the frame. You should have heard him yell. We had to use a pry bar to get him loose. He's fine now, but he's got this gnarly bruise that looks like a map of Texas on his palm. He still showed up to work the next day though, refused to take time off. Old school, you know? They don't make mechanics like that anymore. 

But yeah, the eating... I can't stop. Even when I know I should, even when I feel like garbage, I just can't seem to hit the brakes.
Do you usually feel guilty after these episodes of eating a lot?

Guilty? I mean... I don't know if guilt is the right word. I definitely feel terrible physically, but as for feeling guilty about it... I haven't really thought about it like that. I mostly just feel exhausted and want to go to sleep. 

Speaking of sleep, man, my mattress is completely shot. I’ve had it since I first moved out of my parents' place, which was right after I finished high school and got my first apprenticeship. It’s got this huge dip right in the middle, feels like I’m sleeping in a taco shell. I went to a mattress store last weekend, right? The salesman was pushing this memory foam thing that costs more than my first car. I kept telling him, "Buddy, I sleep on my stomach, I don't need NASA technology, I just need springs that don't stab me." He wouldn't let up though. Reminded me of those snap-on tool truck guys that roll up to the garage every Friday, trying to sell you a ratchet set for a thousand bucks when you can get the job done with a Craftsman half the price. 

But yeah, I don't really know if I feel guilty. I just feel gross and tired.
Do you feel like you're in control of what you're eating during those episodes?

Like I was saying a minute ago, no, I don't have any control at all. It really is like my hands are just operating on their own, grabbing things even when my brain is screaming at me to stop and I'm already feeling totally sick to my stomach. 

Speaking of not having control, you ever see a runaway diesel engine? Man, it is the most terrifying thing. We had this old Cummins come into the shop a few months back, and the seals on the turbo were completely shot. It started sucking its own engine oil into the intake and burning it as fuel. When that happens, turning the ignition key off does absolutely nothing. The engine just keeps revving higher and higher on its own oil, totally out of control, until it literally blows itself to pieces. It sounds like a jet engine taking off right there inside the garage bay. The only way to stop it is to smother the air intake, so my buddy grabbed a heavy shop rag and threw it over the pipe, and the turbo just sucked the rag right in and shredded it. We all just had to run and hide behind the heavy toolboxes until a piston rod shot right through the side of the engine block. Sounded like a shotgun going off. Completely totaled the block. 

But, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, right, the eating. Yeah, no, I'm definitely not in the driver's seat when that happens. Just completely out of my hands.
Do you feel anxious or panicked while you're eating and can't stop?

Anxious? I mean, I guess I get a little worked up, but I wouldn't call it a panic attack or anything. It's more just... frustration, you know? Like, why am I doing this? 

Speaking of frustration, you want to know what really gets my blood boiling? Trying to get parts ordered right now. The supply chain is still completely messed up. I had a guy bring in his Freightliner last week needing a new EGR valve. Used to be, I could call up the distributor, and they'd have it on a truck to me by the afternoon. Now? They're telling me it's on backorder for six weeks. Six weeks! What's this guy supposed to do, just not work for a month and a half? He hauls refrigerated goods, man. Produce, meat, stuff that goes bad. He's losing thousands of dollars every week that truck sits in my bay. And the worst part is, I found the exact part we need sitting in a warehouse in Ohio, but because of some stupid corporate contract BS, my shop isn't allowed to buy from them. We have to use our "approved vendor," who doesn't even have the part! It makes absolutely no sense. I spent three hours on the phone on Tuesday just arguing with this rep who clearly had no idea what an EGR valve even does. 

But yeah, the eating... I don't think I panic. I just get annoyed with myself while it's happening.
Do you enjoy the taste of the food while you're eating during these episodes?

Enjoy it? I mean, maybe for the first bite or two, but honestly, no, I don't really taste it after that. It's just... I'm just shoveling it in, you know? It's not about enjoying a good meal. 

Speaking of a good meal, though, you ever had proper Texas brisket? Because man, I went down to Austin a couple years ago for this diesel mechanics expo, and we hit up this place that had the smokers going out back. The smell alone could knock you out. They smoke it over post oak for like eighteen hours, and when they slice it, it just falls apart. The bark on the outside is all peppery and dark, and the fat just melts. I swear, up here, people think barbecue is just boiling some ribs and slapping sweet baby ray's on it. It's a crime, honestly. I tried to build my own smoker out of an old 55-gallon oil drum last summer. Cleaned it out real good, welded some hinges on, rigged up a firebox on the side. It actually held temperature pretty well, but I couldn't get the airflow right, so the fire kept choking out. Wasted a good thirty-dollar piece of meat trying to figure it out before I just gave up and threw some hot dogs on the regular grill. 

But yeah, the food when I'm eating like that... no, I don't really taste it or enjoy it. It's just going through the motions.
How often do these episodes of eating a lot happen?

Well, it's pretty much an every week thing. Most weeks I'll have at least one night where I just eat like that, completely out of control, and then I have to figure out how to undo it, you know? Like, I'll make myself throw up, or take a bunch of laxatives, or just not eat anything the next day, or go to the gym and just run myself into the ground. It's been happening like this for a few months now. 

Speaking of running things into the ground, I had this guy bring in a Peterbilt last month, right? Beautiful rig, custom paint job, the works. But the guy had completely ignored his maintenance schedule. I'm talking, he hadn't changed the fuel filters in I don't even know how many thousands of miles. The things were practically solid black when I pulled them out. And he was wondering why he was losing power on the hills! I had to explain to him, look, man, these engines are tough, but they need clean fuel. You can't just run them on sludge and expect them to pull forty thousand pounds up a grade. It's like trying to breathe through a wet towel. I spent half the day just cleaning out the fuel lines and the injectors. Honestly, it's a miracle he didn't blow the high-pressure fuel pump. Those things are not cheap to replace, let me tell you. You're talking a couple grand just for the part, not to mention the labor. 

But yeah, the eating thing... at least once a week, and then I do whatever I can to get rid of it. It's been going on for a while.
Do you feel like you're eating in response to emotions or is it more like your body is just going through the motions without any emotional trigger?

I don't really know if there's a specific emotion, honestly. I haven't really thought about it like that. Sometimes I'm stressed, I guess, but other times I just... start. It's like my brain just switches off and I'm just doing it. 

Kind of like when you're driving a familiar route, you know? You ever do that? Where you drive all the way home from work and you pull into the driveway and you realize you don't even remember the last five miles? Highway hypnosis, they call it. I get that sometimes when I have to test drive the rigs after a big repair. We got this stretch of I-95 near the shop, it's just dead straight for like ten miles. Nothing to look at but concrete barriers and the occasional dead deer. I took this Kenworth T680 out last Tuesday—guy said he had a vibration in the steering column at exactly 65 miles an hour. Which, let me tell you, is the most annoying kind of problem to diagnose. Because it could be anything. Could be a tire out of balance, could be a worn kingpin, could be a U-joint starting to go bad on the driveshaft. So I get it up to 65, and sure enough, there's this tiny little shimmy. Just enough to drive you crazy on a long haul. I ended up having to put the front end up on blocks and take a dial indicator to the brake rotors. Turns out one of them was warped just a fraction of an inch. Probably from riding the brakes coming down a mountain pass or something. Some of these guys, they rely too much on the service brakes instead of using the engine brake. Jake brakes are loud, sure, but they save your pads and rotors. 

But yeah, the eating... I don't think it's always an emotional thing. I haven't really noticed a pattern like that. It just happens.
Do you feel like you're able to think clearly about what you're doing while you're eating during these episodes?

No, not really. It's like... once I start on those nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food even while I'm telling myself to stop. And I'm already feeling sick, but I just can't stop my hands from moving. It's like I'm not even in control of my own body anymore. 

It actually reminds me of this time a buddy of mine, Dave, let me drive his old Chevy Nova. It was a '72, I think. Beautiful car, cherry red, but the throttle linkage was all messed up. We were out on this back road, and I gave it some gas, and the pedal just stuck to the floor. I'm talking wide open throttle. I'm yelling, Dave's yelling, the engine is screaming, and I'm standing on the brakes, but the car just wants to keep going. I ended up having to slam it into neutral and coast to a stop on the shoulder, blowing the engine in the process. Dave was so mad, but I told him, man, you gotta maintain your linkages! You can't just slap a big carburetor on there and expect the old hardware to handle it. We spent the whole weekend pulling that motor and trying to salvage the block, but it was totally shot. Had to order a whole new crate engine. 

But yeah, that's kind of what it feels like when I'm eating. Like the pedal is stuck and I'm just along for the ride, even though I know I need to stop.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past few months?

Well, my weight goes up and down a little, but I watch it like a hawk. Even when my work pants feel looser, if I step on the scale and it's up even a single pound, I just panic. I feel like I'm getting fat and I start worrying I'm going to lose control of my whole body, you know? It's terrifying. 

Speaking of losing control of your body, you ever see a guy try to lift a transmission without a proper jack? Man, I saw this kid, new hire at the shop, trying to muscle a heavy-duty Allison transmission onto a workbench all by himself. Those things weigh, like, six, seven hundred pounds easy. I yelled at him to stop, but he already had it halfway up. Next thing you know, his knees buckle, the transmission slips, and he goes down hard. Pinned his leg right under the bell housing. We had to get three guys and a pry bar just to get it off him. He ended up fracturing his tibia in two places. Out on worker's comp for three months. I told the boss, I said, you gotta train these kids better. You can't just throw them in the bay and expect them to know how to use the equipment. We got transmission jacks for a reason! They're on wheels, they got safety chains, you just pump the handle and it does all the work. But no, this kid wanted to be Superman. Now he's walking with a limp and probably will for the rest of his life. It's just stupid, you know? You gotta use the right tools for the job. 

But yeah, the weight thing... if the scale goes up even a pound, I just lose it. I feel like I'm getting huge and everything is spiraling out of control.
Do you ever feel bad about yourself after one of these eating episodes?

Yeah, I do. I feel really disgusted with myself, honestly. Like, I just sit there looking at all the empty wrappers and containers and I just feel so ashamed. It's like, how could I let this happen again, you know? 

It's that same kind of sick feeling you get when you realize you messed up a repair and the customer's already on the road. We had this fleet contract a couple years back, servicing these Peterbilt 389s for a local logging company. Beautiful trucks, classic long-nose style, but they run them hard out in the woods. Mud, rocks, steep grades, you name it. Anyway, I was doing a routine brake job on one of the trailers, replacing the shoes and turning the drums. I thought I had everything buttoned up tight, torqued the lug nuts to spec, the whole nine yards. But I must have gotten distracted, maybe by one of the other guys asking for a tool, because I completely forgot to reinstall the cotter pin on the main slack adjuster clevis. 

So the driver takes the rig out, gets fully loaded with timber, and starts heading down this nasty 6% grade. He hits the brakes, and because that pin was missing, the clevis slips right off. Suddenly he's got zero braking power on that axle. He had to ride the engine brake so hard he almost blew the turbo, and he ended up having to take a runaway truck ramp just to stop the thing. Buried the front end up to the bumper in gravel. When the boss found out it was my bay that truck came out of... man, I felt lower than dirt. I couldn't even look him in the eye. Cost the shop thousands in towing and repairs, not to mention almost getting the driver killed. I didn't sleep for a week after that, just kept replaying it in my head. You have to double-check your work, always. Now I got this habit where I literally touch every single pin and bolt after I install it, just to physically confirm it's there. 

But yeah, that's exactly how I feel after I eat like that. Just this heavy, awful feeling of messing up and being totally ashamed of myself.
You mentioned making yourself throw up after these episodes, is that something you do every time or just sometimes?

Well, it's... I guess I'd say I do it sometimes. After I eat way too much on those nights, I usually end up going to the bathroom to make myself throw up, or sometimes I'll take a bunch of laxatives. I just get so freaked out, you know? Scared of what all that food is going to do to me, to my body. I just have to get it out. 

It's sort of like when you realize you've put the wrong fluid in a system and you just have to flush the whole thing immediately before it destroys the components. Man, I remember this one time, we had a guy bring in his F-350, one of those newer ones with the 6.7 Powerstroke. Beautiful rig, lifted, custom exhaust, the works. He had been trying to do his own maintenance, which, you know, I respect the hustle, but sometimes you gotta know your limits. Anyway, he accidentally topped off his DEF tank—the diesel exhaust fluid—with standard windshield washer fluid. Just poured a whole gallon of the blue stuff right in there. 

I don't know if you know much about modern diesel emissions systems, but the SCR catalyst is incredibly sensitive. You put anything other than pure urea and deionized water in there, and you're looking at a catastrophic failure. I mean, we're talking a five, maybe six thousand dollar repair bill if that washer fluid hits the injector and bakes onto the catalyst. As soon as he told me what he did, I didn't even write up the ticket yet. I just grabbed a pump and shoved a hose down the filler neck. I was siphoning that tank like my life depended on it, trying to get every last drop of that blue garbage out of there. We ended up having to drop the whole tank, flush the lines, replace the DEF pump and the heater assembly just to be safe. It was a nightmare. The guy was practically in tears when he saw the bill, but I told him, buddy, you're lucky you didn't start the engine. If that stuff had cycled through the system, you'd be buying a whole new exhaust setup. 

But yeah, that panic... that need to just purge the system before the damage is done. That's kind of why I do it. I just get so scared of what's going to happen if I don't get rid of it.
Do you always make yourself throw up or use laxatives after these episodes of eating a lot?

Not always, no. Sometimes... well, after a bad night of eating, I’ll just skip breakfast and lunch at work the next day. Or I’ll push myself through extra runs and a bunch of push-ups, even when I’m completely worn out from being on my feet all day. 

And man, being on my feet all day... it really wrecks your joints on that shop concrete. Like, a couple weeks ago we had to do an in-frame rebuild on a Cummins ISX15. You know, rebuilding the engine while it's still sitting right there in the truck chassis. You're constantly climbing up and down the steer tire, leaning over the fender, pulling the heavy-ass cylinder head, dropping the oil pan... it's brutal work. The worst part is pulling the old cylinder liners. They get totally seized up in the block from the heat and carbon, and you have to use this massive puller tool. I was fighting this one liner for like two hours with a breaker bar, just sweating buckets. 

I was on my feet for fourteen hours straight that shift. I buy those expensive Red Wing boots, thinking they'll save my arches, but after fourteen hours on concrete fighting a Cummins block, it doesn't even matter. Your legs just feel like lead, you know? I told the shop manager we need anti-fatigue mats in the heavy bays, but you know how cheap management is. They won't spend a dime unless it makes them a dollar. They think because we're young we can just bounce back, but I see the older guys in the shop walking around with bad knees and blown-out lower backs, and I know that's where I'm headed if I don't watch it. 

But yeah, anyway, even after a grueling shift like that, if I messed up and ate too much the night before, I'll still force myself to go run or do the push-ups. I just skip the meals and grind it out, no matter how dead my legs feel.
Do you often have episodes where you eat a large amount of food in a short time without trying to purge or compensate for it afterwards?

No, I don't think I ever just... leave it alone. Most weeks I have at least one night where I eat like that, just a ton of food, and then I always try to make up for it somehow—throwing up, taking laxatives, skipping meals, or working out extra. It’s been going on for several months now. I just can't let it sit there. 

It’s kind of like when someone ignores a maintenance issue, you know? You can't just pretend it's not there. We had this guy bring in a Freightliner Cascadia a while back, running a Detroit DD15 engine. He knew he had a slow coolant leak. He could see the reservoir dropping, but instead of fixing the root cause, he just kept driving it. Said he was on a tight schedule and didn't have time for downtime. Well, the coolant was leaking internally, right into the oil. If you know anything about heavy-duty engines, coolant and oil make this nasty, milky sludge that completely destroys your lubrication. 

He drove it like that for weeks. Finally, the main bearings just gave out. He spun a bearing going 65 down the interstate and threw a rod right through the side of the engine block. A fifty-dollar gasket leak turned into a thirty-thousand-dollar total engine replacement just because he didn't deal with what was happening inside the system. I spent three whole days just pulling the shattered pieces of that block out of the chassis. The smell of burnt oil and baked antifreeze... man, it is something you never get out of your clothes. I wash my work uniforms separate from my regular clothes, but I swear, my truck still smells like it sometimes. I had to buy these special heavy-duty ozone generators just to get the stench out of the cab of my own pickup... 

But, uh, anyway, what were you asking? Oh, right. Yeah, no, I never just eat all that and do nothing. I always have to make up for it.
Do you ever have episodes where you eat a large amount of food in a short time without feeling a need to purge or compensate for it afterwards?

Wait, didn't I just... I feel like I just answered that, right? But no, I never just eat all that and feel totally fine leaving it alone. The urge to get rid of it is always there. It's like this crazy pressure building up inside my head that I have to release. 

Speaking of pressure, it actually reminds me of how the air brake systems work on these heavy rigs. You've got an engine-mounted air compressor that's governed to cut out at around 120 psi, right? If that governor fails, there's a safety pop-off valve on the primary air tank to keep things from blowing up. Well, last winter, we had this old Peterbilt 379 roll into the shop. The driver had tried to bypass his air dryer because the purge valve kept freezing open. Standard rookie mistake in the cold, honestly. But in doing that, he somehow dead-headed the unloader line. 

So he fires up the truck in our bay to build air, and the compressor just keeps pumping and pumping. The safety valve on the tank was totally corroded shut—which is a massive DOT violation, by the way, the guy should have been put out of service just for that. I was standing maybe ten feet away when the main discharge line literally exploded off the compressor head. Man, it sounded like a 12-gauge shotgun going off indoors. My ears were ringing for three days straight. Our new lube tech, this 19-year-old kid straight out of high school, got so startled he dropped a completely full oil drain pan right onto his own feet. Covered his brand new steel-toes in used 15W-40 diesel oil. I mean, I felt bad for the kid, but it was kind of hilarious. Took him an hour to clean the bay floor with kitty litter. 

But yeah... sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, feeling the need to get rid of the food. Yeah, no, I always feel that pressure. I never just skip doing something about it.
Do you feel like you're in control of your eating during these episodes?

Control? No, not at all. Honestly, once I start on those bad nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food, you know? Like, I'm literally inside my head telling myself to stop, and I’m already feeling physically sick from how much I've had, but I just can't make myself quit. 

It’s like I can't shut the system down once it starts feeding itself. It actually reminds me exactly of a diesel runaway. Have you ever heard of that? It’s probably the most terrifying thing that can happen in a shop. 

See, diesel engines don't use spark plugs like a gas car; they run purely on compression. So if a turbocharger seal blows and starts leaking engine oil into the air intake, the engine will start burning its own motor oil as fuel. You can turn the ignition key completely off, pull it right out of the dash, and the engine will just keep accelerating on its own. It just feeds on itself and you have absolutely zero control over it. The RPMs go way past the redline, the block starts shaking, it sounds like a jet engine about to explode, and the whole shop instantly fills with this thick, blinding white smoke. 

We had an old International box truck do that last summer. The driver brought it in complaining about a weird whistle, and my buddy Dave fired it up in the bay, and bam—instant runaway. The only way to stop it is to completely choke off the air supply. Dave was running around screaming for a piece of plywood or a thick clipboard to slap over the turbo intake. You can't use your hand, because the suction is so strong it'll literally pull your fingers off. We finally jammed a heavy Chilton repair manual over the pipe and it choked out just before the connecting rods decided to launch themselves through the oil pan. Man, my heart was beating out of my chest. 

But, uh... yeah. That feeling where you turn the key off, you know you need to stop, but the engine just keeps screaming anyway? That's... that's kind of what it feels like when I'm eating. I'm telling myself to stop, but my hands just keep going.
Do you feel like you're unable to stop yourself from continuing to eat once you've started eating a large amount of food?

Yeah, I mean, like I was just saying with the runaway engine thing, right? It's exactly that. Once I start on those nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food, even while I’m telling myself to stop. I'll already be feeling completely sick to my stomach from how much I've eaten, but I just can't make myself quit. 

It's honestly a lot like brake fade. You ever drive a heavy rig down a steep mountain pass? If a driver doesn't use their engine brake and just rides the service brakes all the way down, the friction heats the brake drums up to like, 600 degrees. The brake lining actually starts to vaporize, and it creates this pocket of gas between the shoe and the drum. So you're stomping on the pedal, literally standing on it, begging the truck to stop, but there's zero friction. You just keep rolling faster and faster. 

We had this rookie driver in a Kenworth T680 do that coming down a 6% grade last fall. Smoked his brakes so bad he had to use one of those runaway truck ramps. You know, those long uphill gravel pits on the side of the highway? He buried the rig up to the axles in pea gravel. Took two heavy wreckers like five hours just to winch him out of there. The tow bill alone was probably five grand, and that's not even counting the shop time. We had to replace every single brake shoe and drum on the tractor and the trailer. The drums were actually cracked straight through from the thermal shock. 

But, uh... yeah. That feeling of pressing the pedal to the floor and nothing happening? That's what it is. I'm telling myself to stop, I feel sick, but my hands just keep grabbing more food anyway. I just can't stop it.
Do you feel like you have no control over your eating during these episodes?

I feel like we're just going in circles here, doc. I mean, didn't you just ask me that? But yeah, like I said, I have zero control. Once I start on those nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food even while I’m telling myself to stop and I’m already feeling sick. 

It's just... man, it's frustrating, you know? It's like when you're trying to diagnose an electrical short in a modern rig. You think you've got it pinned down, but the CAN bus system is just throwing phantom codes everywhere. Like, last month, we had this Freightliner Cascadia come in. The driver said his wipers would turn on every time he hit the brakes, and the radio would cut out when he used the turn signal. Just completely possessed. 

I spent three days chasing wires. I had the entire dashboard ripped apart, tracing the harness all the way back to the SAM cab module. You know what it ended up being? A single, tiny spot of corrosion on a ground wire behind the driver's seat. The wire had rubbed against a sharp edge on the seat bracket, exposed the copper, and water had wicked up inside the insulation. It was causing a voltage drop that freaked out the whole multiplex system. Three days of my life for a fix that took five minutes and a piece of heat-shrink tubing. I swear, the engineers who design these things have never had to actually turn a wrench on one in the real world. They just sit in their air-conditioned offices... 

Wait, sorry. What were we saying? Oh, right, control. Yeah, no, I don't have any control when I'm eating like that. My hands just keep going, no matter what my brain is saying.
Do you feel like you're unable to stop eating once you've started during these episodes?

Are you messing with me right now? I feel like I'm on a hidden camera show or something. You've literally asked me the exact same question four times in a row, just changing the words around. Yes, like I keep saying, I can't stop. Once I start on those nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food even while I’m telling myself to stop and I’m already feeling sick. 

It's honestly like dealing with a stuck thermostat on an ISX15 Cummins. You know, when the thermostat gets stuck closed and the coolant can't circulate to the radiator? The engine just keeps building heat, and building heat, and there's nowhere for it to go. I had this Peterbilt 389 in the shop a couple months ago, beautiful rig, custom chrome everywhere, and the driver was complaining about it running hot on long pulls. 

I hooked up the diagnostic tool, took it for a test drive, and watched the temp gauge just climb straight to 230 degrees. The fan clutch engaged, sounding like a hurricane under the hood, but it wasn't doing a damn thing because the hot coolant wasn't even reaching the radiator. If I hadn't pulled over and shut it down, it would have cracked the head or blown the head gasket for sure. And replacing a head gasket on one of those is a nightmare. You're talking about draining all the fluids, pulling the turbo, the exhaust manifold, the injectors... it's a solid two days of work just to get down to the block. And don't even get me started on the weight of that cylinder head. You need a cherry picker just to lift it off. 

But yeah, anyway, the point is... I can't stop. The food just keeps going in, and I can't shut it down.

patient.answer:
Hey, doc. Uh, yeah, thanks. I guess I’m here because... well, lately I’ll get off a really long shift at the garage—I work on diesel engines, mostly big rigs and city buses. Man, the buses are the worst. You wouldn’t believe the grease buildup on those transit ones. We had this one come in last Tuesday, transmission was completely shot, and the smell... anyway, my boss expects me to just crank these out, right? 

So I get off work, or I finish up some certification studying I'm trying to do, and I just end up eating way, way more than I planned. Like, I’ll smash a full fast-food meal, then move on to snacks, and basically just eat whatever’s in the fridge, all in one sitting. Which reminds me, my fridge has this weird hum lately, might be the compressor going out. I should probably look at that, but I barely have the energy after wrenching all day, you know? I don't really know if I'm stressed or upset right before, honestly. I haven't really paid much attention to my mood right at that exact minute. I mean, my brain is usually just totally fried by the time I clock out. 

Speaking of fried, the wiring harness on that transit bus I was telling you about? Completely melted. I swear the driver must have ignored the dash warnings for, like, fifty miles. You see that a lot with the city guys, they just push the rigs until they literally start smoking and they have no choice but to pull over. I spent three hours yesterday just splicing in new connections because the whole terminal block was fused together into this giant plastic lump. It's a nightmare trying to trace those schematics. 

But, uh... yeah, to answer your question, I don't really know how I'm feeling before I start eating. I just get home and it happens.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient experiences loss of control during episodes of eating
doctor.question: Do you feel like you can stop eating once you've started on those occasions?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I start on those nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food even while I’m telling myself to stop and I’m already feeling sick.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I feel like I can stop eating once I've started on those occasions, which directly assesses the sense of lack of control over eating during an episode.

patient.answer:
No, man, not at all. Once I start on those nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food even while I’m telling myself to stop. And I'll be sitting there, already feeling sick to my stomach, but I just keep going. It's like I'm on autopilot or something. 

Kind of like this one guy at the shop, Dave. Dave’s been there for like twenty years, right? The guy is practically a machine himself. He can tear down an Allison transmission blindfolded, I swear. But the other day, he was pulling a heavy-duty axle out of a Peterbilt, and he didn't secure the jack right. The whole thing slipped. Bam. Pinched his hand right between the axle and the frame. You should have heard him yell. We had to use a pry bar to get him loose. He's fine now, but he's got this gnarly bruise that looks like a map of Texas on his palm. He still showed up to work the next day though, refused to take time off. Old school, you know? They don't make mechanics like that anymore. 

But yeah, the eating... I can't stop. Even when I know I should, even when I feel like garbage, I just can't seem to hit the brakes.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient experiences guilt after binge eating episodes
doctor.question: Do you usually feel guilty after these episodes of eating a lot?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of guilt after eating episodes, which is a common psychological symptom associated with binge eating, but it is not explicitly covered by any of the provided symptom profiles (such as Compensatory Behaviors, Fear of Weight Gain, or Body Image Disturbance).

patient.answer:
Guilty? I mean... I don't know if guilt is the right word. I definitely feel terrible physically, but as for feeling guilty about it... I haven't really thought about it like that. I mostly just feel exhausted and want to go to sleep. 

Speaking of sleep, man, my mattress is completely shot. I’ve had it since I first moved out of my parents' place, which was right after I finished high school and got my first apprenticeship. It’s got this huge dip right in the middle, feels like I’m sleeping in a taco shell. I went to a mattress store last weekend, right? The salesman was pushing this memory foam thing that costs more than my first car. I kept telling him, "Buddy, I sleep on my stomach, I don't need NASA technology, I just need springs that don't stab me." He wouldn't let up though. Reminded me of those snap-on tool truck guys that roll up to the garage every Friday, trying to sell you a ratchet set for a thousand bucks when you can get the job done with a Craftsman half the price. 

But yeah, I don't really know if I feel guilty. I just feel gross and tired.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient experiences a loss of control during the binge-eating episodes
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're in control of what you're eating during those episodes?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I start on those nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food even while I’m telling myself to stop and I’m already feeling sick.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient feels in control of what they are eating during the episodes, which directly corresponds to the Loss of Control symptom.

patient.answer:
Like I was saying a minute ago, no, I don't have any control at all. It really is like my hands are just operating on their own, grabbing things even when my brain is screaming at me to stop and I'm already feeling totally sick to my stomach. 

Speaking of not having control, you ever see a runaway diesel engine? Man, it is the most terrifying thing. We had this old Cummins come into the shop a few months back, and the seals on the turbo were completely shot. It started sucking its own engine oil into the intake and burning it as fuel. When that happens, turning the ignition key off does absolutely nothing. The engine just keeps revving higher and higher on its own oil, totally out of control, until it literally blows itself to pieces. It sounds like a jet engine taking off right there inside the garage bay. The only way to stop it is to smother the air intake, so my buddy grabbed a heavy shop rag and threw it over the pipe, and the turbo just sucked the rag right in and shredded it. We all just had to run and hide behind the heavy toolboxes until a piston rod shot right through the side of the engine block. Sounded like a shotgun going off. Completely totaled the block. 

But, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, right, the eating. Yeah, no, I'm definitely not in the driver's seat when that happens. Just completely out of my hands.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's loss of control during eating episodes is associated with a sense of anxiety or panic
doctor.question: Do you feel anxious or panicked while you're eating and can't stop?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling anxious or panicked while eating, which is an emotional response during the episode, but does not directly map to the core symptoms of Bulimia Nervosa listed in the profile (such as Loss of Control, which was already addressed, or Compensatory Behaviors). None of the available symptom profiles specifically describe feeling anxious or panicked *while* eating.

patient.answer:
Anxious? I mean, I guess I get a little worked up, but I wouldn't call it a panic attack or anything. It's more just... frustration, you know? Like, why am I doing this? 

Speaking of frustration, you want to know what really gets my blood boiling? Trying to get parts ordered right now. The supply chain is still completely messed up. I had a guy bring in his Freightliner last week needing a new EGR valve. Used to be, I could call up the distributor, and they'd have it on a truck to me by the afternoon. Now? They're telling me it's on backorder for six weeks. Six weeks! What's this guy supposed to do, just not work for a month and a half? He hauls refrigerated goods, man. Produce, meat, stuff that goes bad. He's losing thousands of dollars every week that truck sits in my bay. And the worst part is, I found the exact part we need sitting in a warehouse in Ohio, but because of some stupid corporate contract BS, my shop isn't allowed to buy from them. We have to use our "approved vendor," who doesn't even have the part! It makes absolutely no sense. I spent three hours on the phone on Tuesday just arguing with this rep who clearly had no idea what an EGR valve even does. 

But yeah, the eating... I don't think I panic. I just get annoyed with myself while it's happening.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating episodes are associated with a sense of loss of control and lack of interest in food
doctor.question: Do you enjoy the taste of the food while you're eating during these episodes?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether I enjoy the taste of the food during the binge eating episodes, which is not specifically covered by any of the symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Enjoy it? I mean, maybe for the first bite or two, but honestly, no, I don't really taste it after that. It's just... I'm just shoveling it in, you know? It's not about enjoying a good meal. 

Speaking of a good meal, though, you ever had proper Texas brisket? Because man, I went down to Austin a couple years ago for this diesel mechanics expo, and we hit up this place that had the smokers going out back. The smell alone could knock you out. They smoke it over post oak for like eighteen hours, and when they slice it, it just falls apart. The bark on the outside is all peppery and dark, and the fat just melts. I swear, up here, people think barbecue is just boiling some ribs and slapping sweet baby ray's on it. It's a crime, honestly. I tried to build my own smoker out of an old 55-gallon oil drum last summer. Cleaned it out real good, welded some hinges on, rigged up a firebox on the side. It actually held temperature pretty well, but I couldn't get the airflow right, so the fire kept choking out. Wasted a good thirty-dollar piece of meat trying to figure it out before I just gave up and threw some hot dogs on the regular grill. 

But yeah, the food when I'm eating like that... no, I don't really taste it or enjoy it. It's just going through the motions.

doctor.intent: determine frequency of episodes
doctor.question: How often do these episodes of eating a lot happen?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Most weeks I have at least one night where I eat like that and then try to make up for it by throwing up, taking laxatives, skipping meals, or working out extra, and it’s been going on for several months now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the frequency of the binge eating episodes, which is covered by the additional requirement regarding the frequency of binge eating and compensatory behaviors.

patient.answer:
Well, it's pretty much an every week thing. Most weeks I'll have at least one night where I just eat like that, completely out of control, and then I have to figure out how to undo it, you know? Like, I'll make myself throw up, or take a bunch of laxatives, or just not eat anything the next day, or go to the gym and just run myself into the ground. It's been happening like this for a few months now. 

Speaking of running things into the ground, I had this guy bring in a Peterbilt last month, right? Beautiful rig, custom paint job, the works. But the guy had completely ignored his maintenance schedule. I'm talking, he hadn't changed the fuel filters in I don't even know how many thousands of miles. The things were practically solid black when I pulled them out. And he was wondering why he was losing power on the hills! I had to explain to him, look, man, these engines are tough, but they need clean fuel. You can't just run them on sludge and expect them to pull forty thousand pounds up a grade. It's like trying to breathe through a wet towel. I spent half the day just cleaning out the fuel lines and the injectors. Honestly, it's a miracle he didn't blow the high-pressure fuel pump. Those things are not cheap to replace, let me tell you. You're talking a couple grand just for the part, not to mention the labor. 

But yeah, the eating thing... at least once a week, and then I do whatever I can to get rid of it. It's been going on for a while.

doctor.intent: determine if patient's eating episodes are accompanied by a sense of loss of control and lack of enjoyment
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're eating in response to emotions or is it more like your body is just going through the motions without any emotional trigger?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about emotional triggers for the eating episodes, which is not specifically covered by any of the symptom profile items (such as loss of control or eating a large amount).

patient.answer:
I don't really know if there's a specific emotion, honestly. I haven't really thought about it like that. Sometimes I'm stressed, I guess, but other times I just... start. It's like my brain just switches off and I'm just doing it. 

Kind of like when you're driving a familiar route, you know? You ever do that? Where you drive all the way home from work and you pull into the driveway and you realize you don't even remember the last five miles? Highway hypnosis, they call it. I get that sometimes when I have to test drive the rigs after a big repair. We got this stretch of I-95 near the shop, it's just dead straight for like ten miles. Nothing to look at but concrete barriers and the occasional dead deer. I took this Kenworth T680 out last Tuesday—guy said he had a vibration in the steering column at exactly 65 miles an hour. Which, let me tell you, is the most annoying kind of problem to diagnose. Because it could be anything. Could be a tire out of balance, could be a worn kingpin, could be a U-joint starting to go bad on the driveshaft. So I get it up to 65, and sure enough, there's this tiny little shimmy. Just enough to drive you crazy on a long haul. I ended up having to put the front end up on blocks and take a dial indicator to the brake rotors. Turns out one of them was warped just a fraction of an inch. Probably from riding the brakes coming down a mountain pass or something. Some of these guys, they rely too much on the service brakes instead of using the engine brake. Jake brakes are loud, sure, but they save your pads and rotors. 

But yeah, the eating... I don't think it's always an emotional thing. I haven't really noticed a pattern like that. It just happens.

doctor.intent: determine if patient's eating episodes are accompanied by a sense of loss of control
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're able to think clearly about what you're doing while you're eating during these episodes?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I start on those nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food even while I’m telling myself to stop and I’m already feeling sick.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question about being able to think clearly about what the patient is doing during the eating episodes is assessing the patient's sense of control or lack thereof over their eating.

patient.answer:
No, not really. It's like... once I start on those nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food even while I'm telling myself to stop. And I'm already feeling sick, but I just can't stop my hands from moving. It's like I'm not even in control of my own body anymore. 

It actually reminds me of this time a buddy of mine, Dave, let me drive his old Chevy Nova. It was a '72, I think. Beautiful car, cherry red, but the throttle linkage was all messed up. We were out on this back road, and I gave it some gas, and the pedal just stuck to the floor. I'm talking wide open throttle. I'm yelling, Dave's yelling, the engine is screaming, and I'm standing on the brakes, but the car just wants to keep going. I ended up having to slam it into neutral and coast to a stop on the shoulder, blowing the engine in the process. Dave was so mad, but I told him, man, you gotta maintain your linkages! You can't just slap a big carburetor on there and expect the old hardware to handle it. We spent the whole weekend pulling that motor and trying to salvage the block, but it was totally shot. Had to order a whole new crate engine. 

But yeah, that's kind of what it feels like when I'm eating. Like the pedal is stuck and I'm just along for the ride, even though I know I need to stop.

doctor.intent: determine if patient experiences weight fluctuations due to binge eating
doctor.question: Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past few months?

target_item.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
target_item.manifestation: Even when my work pants are looser, if the scale is up even a pound I feel like I’m getting fat and I start worrying I’m going to lose control of my whole body.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in weight, which naturally prompts the patient to discuss their hyper-focus on the scale, weight fluctuations, and the intense fear of gaining weight as described in S045.

patient.answer:
Well, my weight goes up and down a little, but I watch it like a hawk. Even when my work pants feel looser, if I step on the scale and it's up even a single pound, I just panic. I feel like I'm getting fat and I start worrying I'm going to lose control of my whole body, you know? It's terrifying. 

Speaking of losing control of your body, you ever see a guy try to lift a transmission without a proper jack? Man, I saw this kid, new hire at the shop, trying to muscle a heavy-duty Allison transmission onto a workbench all by himself. Those things weigh, like, six, seven hundred pounds easy. I yelled at him to stop, but he already had it halfway up. Next thing you know, his knees buckle, the transmission slips, and he goes down hard. Pinned his leg right under the bell housing. We had to get three guys and a pry bar just to get it off him. He ended up fracturing his tibia in two places. Out on worker's comp for three months. I told the boss, I said, you gotta train these kids better. You can't just throw them in the bay and expect them to know how to use the equipment. We got transmission jacks for a reason! They're on wheels, they got safety chains, you just pump the handle and it does all the work. But no, this kid wanted to be Superman. Now he's walking with a limp and probably will for the rest of his life. It's just stupid, you know? You gotta use the right tools for the job. 

But yeah, the weight thing... if the scale goes up even a pound, I just lose it. I feel like I'm getting huge and everything is spiraling out of control.

doctor.intent: determine if patient's eating episodes are accompanied by a sense of guilt or self-criticism afterwards
doctor.question: Do you ever feel bad about yourself after one of these eating episodes?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of guilt or shame after eating episodes, which does not directly match the remaining symptom profiles (S046 is specifically about body weight/shape influencing self-evaluation, and S047/S048 are about compensatory behaviors).

patient.answer:
Yeah, I do. I feel really disgusted with myself, honestly. Like, I just sit there looking at all the empty wrappers and containers and I just feel so ashamed. It's like, how could I let this happen again, you know? 

It's that same kind of sick feeling you get when you realize you messed up a repair and the customer's already on the road. We had this fleet contract a couple years back, servicing these Peterbilt 389s for a local logging company. Beautiful trucks, classic long-nose style, but they run them hard out in the woods. Mud, rocks, steep grades, you name it. Anyway, I was doing a routine brake job on one of the trailers, replacing the shoes and turning the drums. I thought I had everything buttoned up tight, torqued the lug nuts to spec, the whole nine yards. But I must have gotten distracted, maybe by one of the other guys asking for a tool, because I completely forgot to reinstall the cotter pin on the main slack adjuster clevis. 

So the driver takes the rig out, gets fully loaded with timber, and starts heading down this nasty 6% grade. He hits the brakes, and because that pin was missing, the clevis slips right off. Suddenly he's got zero braking power on that axle. He had to ride the engine brake so hard he almost blew the turbo, and he ended up having to take a runaway truck ramp just to stop the thing. Buried the front end up to the bumper in gravel. When the boss found out it was my bay that truck came out of... man, I felt lower than dirt. I couldn't even look him in the eye. Cost the shop thousands in towing and repairs, not to mention almost getting the driver killed. I didn't sleep for a week after that, just kept replaying it in my head. You have to double-check your work, always. Now I got this habit where I literally touch every single pin and bolt after I install it, just to physically confirm it's there. 

But yeah, that's exactly how I feel after I eat like that. Just this heavy, awful feeling of messing up and being totally ashamed of myself.

doctor.intent: determine if patient's eating episodes are followed by purging behaviors
doctor.question: You mentioned making yourself throw up after these episodes, is that something you do every time or just sometimes?

target_item.name: Compensatory_Behavior_Purging
target_item.manifestation: Sometimes after I eat too much, I go to the bathroom and make myself throw up, or I take laxatives because I’m scared of what the food is going to do to me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's behavior of making himself throw up after eating episodes, which corresponds to purging compensatory behaviors.

patient.answer:
Well, it's... I guess I'd say I do it sometimes. After I eat way too much on those nights, I usually end up going to the bathroom to make myself throw up, or sometimes I'll take a bunch of laxatives. I just get so freaked out, you know? Scared of what all that food is going to do to me, to my body. I just have to get it out. 

It's sort of like when you realize you've put the wrong fluid in a system and you just have to flush the whole thing immediately before it destroys the components. Man, I remember this one time, we had a guy bring in his F-350, one of those newer ones with the 6.7 Powerstroke. Beautiful rig, lifted, custom exhaust, the works. He had been trying to do his own maintenance, which, you know, I respect the hustle, but sometimes you gotta know your limits. Anyway, he accidentally topped off his DEF tank—the diesel exhaust fluid—with standard windshield washer fluid. Just poured a whole gallon of the blue stuff right in there. 

I don't know if you know much about modern diesel emissions systems, but the SCR catalyst is incredibly sensitive. You put anything other than pure urea and deionized water in there, and you're looking at a catastrophic failure. I mean, we're talking a five, maybe six thousand dollar repair bill if that washer fluid hits the injector and bakes onto the catalyst. As soon as he told me what he did, I didn't even write up the ticket yet. I just grabbed a pump and shoved a hose down the filler neck. I was siphoning that tank like my life depended on it, trying to get every last drop of that blue garbage out of there. We ended up having to drop the whole tank, flush the lines, replace the DEF pump and the heater assembly just to be safe. It was a nightmare. The guy was practically in tears when he saw the bill, but I told him, buddy, you're lucky you didn't start the engine. If that stuff had cycled through the system, you'd be buying a whole new exhaust setup. 

But yeah, that panic... that need to just purge the system before the damage is done. That's kind of why I do it. I just get so scared of what's going to happen if I don't get rid of it.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating episodes are followed by compensatory behaviors consistently
doctor.question: Do you always make yourself throw up or use laxatives after these episodes of eating a lot?

target_item.name: Compensatory_Behavior_NonPurging
target_item.manifestation: After a bad night of eating, I’ll skip breakfast and lunch at work or push myself through extra runs and push-ups even when I’m worn out from being on my feet all day.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if purging is the only method used after binge eating, which provides the opportunity to discuss non-purging compensatory behaviors like fasting and excessive exercise.

patient.answer:
Not always, no. Sometimes... well, after a bad night of eating, I’ll just skip breakfast and lunch at work the next day. Or I’ll push myself through extra runs and a bunch of push-ups, even when I’m completely worn out from being on my feet all day. 

And man, being on my feet all day... it really wrecks your joints on that shop concrete. Like, a couple weeks ago we had to do an in-frame rebuild on a Cummins ISX15. You know, rebuilding the engine while it's still sitting right there in the truck chassis. You're constantly climbing up and down the steer tire, leaning over the fender, pulling the heavy-ass cylinder head, dropping the oil pan... it's brutal work. The worst part is pulling the old cylinder liners. They get totally seized up in the block from the heat and carbon, and you have to use this massive puller tool. I was fighting this one liner for like two hours with a breaker bar, just sweating buckets. 

I was on my feet for fourteen hours straight that shift. I buy those expensive Red Wing boots, thinking they'll save my arches, but after fourteen hours on concrete fighting a Cummins block, it doesn't even matter. Your legs just feel like lead, you know? I told the shop manager we need anti-fatigue mats in the heavy bays, but you know how cheap management is. They won't spend a dime unless it makes them a dollar. They think because we're young we can just bounce back, but I see the older guys in the shop walking around with bad knees and blown-out lower backs, and I know that's where I'm headed if I don't watch it. 

But yeah, anyway, even after a grueling shift like that, if I messed up and ate too much the night before, I'll still force myself to go run or do the push-ups. I just skip the meals and grind it out, no matter how dead my legs feel.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's behavior is more aligned with Other Specified Feeding or Eating Disorder (F50.8) or Unspecified Feeding or Eating Disorder (F50.9) based on the presence of recurrent episodes of binge eating without other compensatory behaviors
doctor.question: Do you often have episodes where you eat a large amount of food in a short time without trying to purge or compensate for it afterwards?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the frequency of binge eating episodes occurring without compensatory behaviors, which prompts the patient to clarify how often the binge eating and compensatory behaviors occur together, addressing the frequency and duration criteria.

patient.answer:
No, I don't think I ever just... leave it alone. Most weeks I have at least one night where I eat like that, just a ton of food, and then I always try to make up for it somehow—throwing up, taking laxatives, skipping meals, or working out extra. It’s been going on for several months now. I just can't let it sit there. 

It’s kind of like when someone ignores a maintenance issue, you know? You can't just pretend it's not there. We had this guy bring in a Freightliner Cascadia a while back, running a Detroit DD15 engine. He knew he had a slow coolant leak. He could see the reservoir dropping, but instead of fixing the root cause, he just kept driving it. Said he was on a tight schedule and didn't have time for downtime. Well, the coolant was leaking internally, right into the oil. If you know anything about heavy-duty engines, coolant and oil make this nasty, milky sludge that completely destroys your lubrication. 

He drove it like that for weeks. Finally, the main bearings just gave out. He spun a bearing going 65 down the interstate and threw a rod right through the side of the engine block. A fifty-dollar gasket leak turned into a thirty-thousand-dollar total engine replacement just because he didn't deal with what was happening inside the system. I spent three whole days just pulling the shattered pieces of that block out of the chassis. The smell of burnt oil and baked antifreeze... man, it is something you never get out of your clothes. I wash my work uniforms separate from my regular clothes, but I swear, my truck still smells like it sometimes. I had to buy these special heavy-duty ozone generators just to get the stench out of the cab of my own pickup... 

But, uh, anyway, what were you asking? Oh, right. Yeah, no, I never just eat all that and do nothing. I always have to make up for it.

doctor.question: Do you ever have episodes where you eat a large amount of food in a short time without feeling a need to purge or compensate for it afterwards?

This does not map to any remaining unaddressed symptoms in the profile, such as loss of control, fear of weight gain, or body image disturbance.

patient.answer:
Wait, didn't I just... I feel like I just answered that, right? But no, I never just eat all that and feel totally fine leaving it alone. The urge to get rid of it is always there. It's like this crazy pressure building up inside my head that I have to release. 

Speaking of pressure, it actually reminds me of how the air brake systems work on these heavy rigs. You've got an engine-mounted air compressor that's governed to cut out at around 120 psi, right? If that governor fails, there's a safety pop-off valve on the primary air tank to keep things from blowing up. Well, last winter, we had this old Peterbilt 379 roll into the shop. The driver had tried to bypass his air dryer because the purge valve kept freezing open. Standard rookie mistake in the cold, honestly. But in doing that, he somehow dead-headed the unloader line. 

So he fires up the truck in our bay to build air, and the compressor just keeps pumping and pumping. The safety valve on the tank was totally corroded shut—which is a massive DOT violation, by the way, the guy should have been put out of service just for that. I was standing maybe ten feet away when the main discharge line literally exploded off the compressor head. Man, it sounded like a 12-gauge shotgun going off indoors. My ears were ringing for three days straight. Our new lube tech, this 19-year-old kid straight out of high school, got so startled he dropped a completely full oil drain pan right onto his own feet. Covered his brand new steel-toes in used 15W-40 diesel oil. I mean, I felt bad for the kid, but it was kind of hilarious. Took him an hour to clean the bay floor with kitty litter. 

But yeah... sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, feeling the need to get rid of the food. Yeah, no, I always feel that pressure. I never just skip doing something about it.

doctor.question: Do you feel like you're in control of your eating during these episodes?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I start on those nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food even while I’m telling myself to stop and I’m already feeling sick.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about the patient's feeling of control over their eating during the episodes, which matches the Loss_of_Control symptom.

patient.answer:
Control? No, not at all. Honestly, once I start on those bad nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food, you know? Like, I'm literally inside my head telling myself to stop, and I’m already feeling physically sick from how much I've had, but I just can't make myself quit. 

It’s like I can't shut the system down once it starts feeding itself. It actually reminds me exactly of a diesel runaway. Have you ever heard of that? It’s probably the most terrifying thing that can happen in a shop. 

See, diesel engines don't use spark plugs like a gas car; they run purely on compression. So if a turbocharger seal blows and starts leaking engine oil into the air intake, the engine will start burning its own motor oil as fuel. You can turn the ignition key completely off, pull it right out of the dash, and the engine will just keep accelerating on its own. It just feeds on itself and you have absolutely zero control over it. The RPMs go way past the redline, the block starts shaking, it sounds like a jet engine about to explode, and the whole shop instantly fills with this thick, blinding white smoke. 

We had an old International box truck do that last summer. The driver brought it in complaining about a weird whistle, and my buddy Dave fired it up in the bay, and bam—instant runaway. The only way to stop it is to completely choke off the air supply. Dave was running around screaming for a piece of plywood or a thick clipboard to slap over the turbo intake. You can't use your hand, because the suction is so strong it'll literally pull your fingers off. We finally jammed a heavy Chilton repair manual over the pipe and it choked out just before the connecting rods decided to launch themselves through the oil pan. Man, my heart was beating out of my chest. 

But, uh... yeah. That feeling where you turn the key off, you know you need to stop, but the engine just keeps screaming anyway? That's... that's kind of what it feels like when I'm eating. I'm telling myself to stop, but my hands just keep going.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean, like I was just saying with the runaway engine thing, right? It's exactly that. Once I start on those nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food, even while I’m telling myself to stop. I'll already be feeling completely sick to my stomach from how much I've eaten, but I just can't make myself quit. 

It's honestly a lot like brake fade. You ever drive a heavy rig down a steep mountain pass? If a driver doesn't use their engine brake and just rides the service brakes all the way down, the friction heats the brake drums up to like, 600 degrees. The brake lining actually starts to vaporize, and it creates this pocket of gas between the shoe and the drum. So you're stomping on the pedal, literally standing on it, begging the truck to stop, but there's zero friction. You just keep rolling faster and faster. 

We had this rookie driver in a Kenworth T680 do that coming down a 6% grade last fall. Smoked his brakes so bad he had to use one of those runaway truck ramps. You know, those long uphill gravel pits on the side of the highway? He buried the rig up to the axles in pea gravel. Took two heavy wreckers like five hours just to winch him out of there. The tow bill alone was probably five grand, and that's not even counting the shop time. We had to replace every single brake shoe and drum on the tractor and the trailer. The drums were actually cracked straight through from the thermal shock. 

But, uh... yeah. That feeling of pressing the pedal to the floor and nothing happening? That's what it is. I'm telling myself to stop, I feel sick, but my hands just keep grabbing more food anyway. I just can't stop it.

patient.answer:
I feel like we're just going in circles here, doc. I mean, didn't you just ask me that? But yeah, like I said, I have zero control. Once I start on those nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food even while I’m telling myself to stop and I’m already feeling sick. 

It's just... man, it's frustrating, you know? It's like when you're trying to diagnose an electrical short in a modern rig. You think you've got it pinned down, but the CAN bus system is just throwing phantom codes everywhere. Like, last month, we had this Freightliner Cascadia come in. The driver said his wipers would turn on every time he hit the brakes, and the radio would cut out when he used the turn signal. Just completely possessed. 

I spent three days chasing wires. I had the entire dashboard ripped apart, tracing the harness all the way back to the SAM cab module. You know what it ended up being? A single, tiny spot of corrosion on a ground wire behind the driver's seat. The wire had rubbed against a sharp edge on the seat bracket, exposed the copper, and water had wicked up inside the insulation. It was causing a voltage drop that freaked out the whole multiplex system. Three days of my life for a fix that took five minutes and a piece of heat-shrink tubing. I swear, the engineers who design these things have never had to actually turn a wrench on one in the real world. They just sit in their air-conditioned offices... 

Wait, sorry. What were we saying? Oh, right, control. Yeah, no, I don't have any control when I'm eating like that. My hands just keep going, no matter what my brain is saying.

patient.answer:
Are you messing with me right now? I feel like I'm on a hidden camera show or something. You've literally asked me the exact same question four times in a row, just changing the words around. Yes, like I keep saying, I can't stop. Once I start on those nights, it feels like my hands just keep grabbing food even while I’m telling myself to stop and I’m already feeling sick. 

It's honestly like dealing with a stuck thermostat on an ISX15 Cummins. You know, when the thermostat gets stuck closed and the coolant can't circulate to the radiator? The engine just keeps building heat, and building heat, and there's nowhere for it to go. I had this Peterbilt 389 in the shop a couple months ago, beautiful rig, custom chrome everywhere, and the driver was complaining about it running hot on long pulls. 

I hooked up the diagnostic tool, took it for a test drive, and watched the temp gauge just climb straight to 230 degrees. The fan clutch engaged, sounding like a hurricane under the hood, but it wasn't doing a damn thing because the hot coolant wasn't even reaching the radiator. If I hadn't pulled over and shut it down, it would have cracked the head or blown the head gasket for sure. And replacing a head gasket on one of those is a nightmare. You're talking about draining all the fluids, pulling the turbo, the exhaust manifold, the injectors... it's a solid two days of work just to get down to the block. And don't even get me started on the weight of that cylinder head. You need a cherry picker just to lift it off. 

But yeah, anyway, the point is... I can't stop. The food just keeps going in, and I can't shut it down.
